html:
In 1951 India began the first of its Five-Year Plans. For forty years the state decided where the country's money would be invested, built the heavy industries itself and controlled private business by licence.

Nehru admired Soviet planning and distrusted the free market, which he linked with colonial rule. He set up the Planning Commission in 1950 and chaired it himself.

The First Plan, to 1956, went mainly to farming, dams and canals (see Bhakra Dam). The Second, drawn up by the statistician P. C. Mahalanobis, put steel and machines first: build the industries that make machines and the rest will follow. Three state steel plants rose, at Bhilai with Soviet help, Rourkela with German and Durgapur with British. Nehru called such works the temples of modern India.

Private firms needed a licence to open a plant, expand it or import parts. Imports were kept out by high tariffs. Critics named the system the Licence Raj. It built an industrial base and trained engineers, and it bred delay, shortages and bribery. Growth averaged about 3.5 per cent a year for three decades.

A payments crisis in 1991 ended the model (see economic liberalisation). The Planning Commission was closed in 2015.
sum: In 1951 India began the first of its Five-Year Plans. For forty years the state decided where the country's money would be invested, built the heavy industries itself and controlled private business by licence.
